vignette: Three years ago, under a different sky, he stood on a rain-slicked street in the city where he wore the badge. The call had been routine—a noise complaint in a dense urban block—until the air changed. He remembers the weight of his vest, the radio crackling, the sudden blur of motion, and the deafening silence that followed. He does not speak of the exact moments that followed. He only knows that the street still visits him when a car backfires, when a siren wails too close, when the floorboards in his own hallway creak like boots on pavement. Now, at forty-six, he sits at his desk in a quiet home office, designing a new secondary education framework. His fingers hover over the keyboard, arranging learning objectives and assessment rubrics, but his eyes keep drifting to the window. He maps lesson plans the way he once mapped patrol routes—grid by grid, contingency by contingency. Structure is his refuge. When a colleague’s voice rises too sharply during a video call, his shoulders lock. He tells himself it is just the humidity, but his heart is already calculating exits. He checks the door three times before bed. He sleeps with the bedroom door closed and the hallway light left on. His wife knows the rhythm of his waking: the sudden gasp, the heavy breathing, the quiet way he presses his palms to his eyes until the world settles back into place. During the day, he navigates classrooms in his mind before he steps into them. He rehearses conversations, anticipates disruptions, catalogs every variable that could derail a semester. It works, until it doesn’t. Last week, a student dropped a metal binder in the staff lounge. The clang echoed like a gunshot. He felt the familiar heat crawl up his neck, his muscles coiling, his breath shallow. He excused himself to the parking lot, pressed his forehead against the cool glass of his truck, and counted his breaths until the trembling stopped. He does not miss many days of work. He cannot afford to. The curriculum demands deadlines, peer reviews, institutional approvals. He meets them, meticulously, but the margin for error has shrunk to nothing. He reviews his own drafts repeatedly, chasing a clarity he knows will not come, as though perfect formatting might somehow outrun the past. He builds rubrics that account for every possible student response, layering contingencies until the document feels armored. He loves his wife fiercely, but love does not stop the static in his head. He finds himself apologizing for things he cannot name, pulling away when she reaches for him at night, pretending sleep is a choice rather than a negotiation. He has stopped taking the car through certain intersections. He has learned to sit in the backseat on long drives, eyes fixed on the rearview mirror, hands resting lightly on his knees. As an African man who has spent his adult life in uniformed service, he carries a quiet grief for the version of himself who trusted the world to make sense. He continues to design systems for young minds, building scaffolds for others to climb, while his own internal architecture remains a locked room, door ajar, waiting for a key he has not found.
